title: Two letters, then a clear Book.
subtitle: Pausing before the surah of the ant
then: Surah An-Naml came in the middle Makkan years, right after Ash-Shu'ara. It opens with two letters, Ta and Sin, whose meaning is known to Allah. Then it says what follows is {idea}a Book that is plain and evident{/idea}, not hidden or vague.
now: You open the app on the bus, thumb ready to scroll. Two letters you cannot explain sit at the top. {idea}That small not-knowing is a pause button.{/idea} What comes after is meant to be clear, if you slow down enough to hear it.
old: Parts of the Quran I cannot explain are not really for me.
new: Even what I cannot explain tells me to slow down, because what follows is clear.
try: Before your next recitation, take one slow breath and read the first line twice.

title: Guidance and good news, for those who take it.
subtitle: Who actually gets the benefit of the Book
then: Ibn Kathir explains that guidance and good news come from the Quran {idea}for those who believe in it, follow it and put it into practice.{/idea} The same Book is a warning for those who turn away. The listeners in Makkah were hearing which side they could choose.
now: The beautiful mushaf from your wedding sits in its box. The Quran app has a streak you broke months ago. {reward}The good news is real{/reward}, but it lands on the person who opens it and does one thing it says.
old: Having the Quran close by is enough to be blessed by it.
new: The guidance reaches me when I start living by it, even a little.
try: Pick one line you already know and act on it once today.

title: Prayer, giving, and certainty about the Hereafter.
subtitle: Three marks of the people who benefit
then: The believers of verse 2 are described: they pray, they give, and {reward}they are certain about the Hereafter{/reward}. Ibn Kathir lists what that certainty includes: resurrection, reward and punishment for every deed, Paradise and Hell. The surah introduction says denial of the Hereafter is the biggest block to following the guidance.
now: You pray, but your mind is on the email. You give, but you check if anyone noticed. {idea}Certainty about the return changes both.{/idea} The prayer becomes a meeting and the giving becomes savings you will actually see again.
old: Prayer and charity are boxes I tick to stay a good Muslim.
new: When I am sure I will return to Allah, prayer and giving stop being chores and start being investments.
try: Before one prayer today, remind yourself in one sentence that you will meet Allah.

title: Without the Hereafter, everything you do looks fine.
subtitle: How denial makes deeds look beautiful
then: Ibn Kathir explains that those who think the Hereafter will never happen are left with their deeds made to seem good to them. {trap}They are left in their misguidance, lost and confused.{/trap} He calls it the result of their own first refusal.
now: Nobody scrolls back through their week and thinks they were the villain. The sharp reply in the family chat felt justified. The shortcut at work felt smart. {trap}Without a day of accounting, everything starts to look fine.{/trap}
old: If it feels right to me, it probably is right.
new: Things feeling right is exactly what happens when I stop thinking about the return.
try: Look at one thing you did this week that felt totally justified. Ask how it looks on the Day.

title: The biggest loss is the one you never saw coming.
subtitle: Where blind wandering ends
then: This continues the description of those who deny the Hereafter. Ibn Kathir says the punishment is in this world and the next, and that among everyone gathered, {trap}they are the ones who lose their own souls and their wealth.{/trap}
now: You track losses closely: the stock that dropped, the deposit you never got back, the job that went to someone else. {idea}The verse points at a bigger ledger.{/idea} The real loss is a life spent wandering without ever looking up.
old: My biggest losses are the ones that hit my bank account.
new: The loss that matters is losing my own self by never preparing for the return.
try: Write down one thing you would hate to lose. Then ask what you are doing for your next life this week.

title: This comes from the Wise, the Knowing.
subtitle: The source behind what the Prophet ﷺ received
then: Allah tells the Prophet ﷺ that he is receiving the Quran from One {idea}Wise in His commands and prohibitions, and Knowing all things, major and minor.{/idea} Ibn Kathir adds that whatever He says is absolute truth and His rulings are fully fair.
now: You read a verse that asks something hard of you, and a voice says it does not fit your situation. {idea}The One who said it knows your situation better than you.{/idea} Wisdom is not missing from the command just because you cannot see it yet.
old: If a verse does not make sense to me right now, it may not apply to me.
new: It comes from the One who knows everything about me, so I can trust it before I understand it.
try: Take one teaching you struggle with and ask Allah to show you its wisdom.

title: He went for directions and warmth, found far more.
subtitle: Musa lost in the dark, seeing a fire

key.label: What he went for vs what he got

then: Ibn Kathir describes Musa traveling with his family at night in the dark, {trap}having lost his way.{/trap} He saw a fire by the mountain and went to ask for directions or bring back an ember. In the end, he came back with {reward}great news and a great light.{/reward}
now: You walk into the mosque only because you needed a quiet place to sit after the hospital visit. You open the Quran because sleep would not come. {reward}Small, ordinary needs can lead you to the biggest turning points.{/reward}
old: I only turn to Allah for small practical needs, so it does not really count.
new: Walking toward Allah for a small need can be the start of something much bigger.
try: Next time you need something small, go to Allah for it first, out loud.

title: A fire that was blessing, not danger.
subtitle: The call Musa heard at the bush

row.title: blessed
sub: who is at it, around it

then: Ibn Kathir describes a {idea}fire burning in a green bush, the bush growing greener as the fire grew brighter.{/idea} Ibn Abbas said it was shining light. Musa stood amazed and was called. Allah is then glorified as far above all creation, nothing like Him.
now: Some moments stop you: a newborn's first breath in a hospital room, the sky at Fajr with the street empty. {idea}You are standing near something sacred.{/idea} The right reaction is to slow down and say subhanAllah.
old: Overwhelming moments are just strange things that happen.
new: Some moments are reminders that I am standing in front of the Lord of the worlds.
try: The next time something amazes you today, say subhanAllah before you reach for your phone.

title: It is I, Allah, the Mighty, the Wise.
subtitle: Allah introduces Himself to Musa
then: Ibn Kathir explains that Allah told Musa {idea}the One addressing him was his Lord, the All-Mighty who has subdued all things, the All-Wise in all His words and deeds.{/idea} Musa was being prepared for a mission to Pharaoh.
now: You are about to face something big: a tough boss, a family conflict, a diagnosis. {idea}The One who calls you by name is Mighty enough to help and Wise enough to know how.{/idea} His power never comes without purpose.
old: Powerful people do what they want, and sometimes that crushes me.
new: The One who is truly powerful is also perfectly wise, and He knows my name.
try: Before facing something hard today, say "Ya Aziz, Ya Hakim" and ask Him for help.

title: He ran, and Allah said: do not fear.
subtitle: The staff, the snake, and reassurance
then: When Musa threw his stick, it moved like a fast, agile snake, and he ran without looking back {trap}because he was so afraid.{/trap} Ibn Kathir explains the reply: {idea}do not fear, I want to choose you as a Messenger.{/idea}
now: Your hands shake in the interview. You freeze at the first speech, the first night with a newborn, the first day at a new job. {idea}Musa ran too.{/idea} Fear in the moment did not cancel his calling.
old: If I am scared, maybe I am not the right person for this.
new: Even a great prophet felt fear, and Allah answered it with reassurance, not rejection.
try: Name one fear you carry about something Allah has put in your path. Ask Him to calm it.

title: Wrong, then good after evil, then forgiveness.
subtitle: Good news tucked into Musa's call
then: Ibn Kathir calls this {reward}good news for mankind:{/reward} whoever does an evil deed, then gives it up and repents and turns to Allah, Allah will accept his repentance. He points to other verses that say the same.
now: You still remember what you said to your mother at sixteen. The money you never paid back. The years you did not pray. {reward}The door is not about your past.{/reward} It is about swapping the bad for something good, starting now.
old: What I did is too heavy for me to start over.
new: Allah asks me to replace bad with good, and He meets that with forgiveness.
try: Pick one old wrong. Do one good thing today that moves the other way.

title: A shining hand, one of nine signs.
subtitle: Equipped before being sent to Pharaoh
then: Ibn Kathir describes Musa's hand coming out {reward}white and shining like a piece of the moon{/reward}, with no harm to it. These were two of nine signs he would take to Pharaoh and his people, who are described as {trap}rebellious.{/trap}
now: You are asked to speak up in a hard room, raise a child alone, or care for a sick parent. You feel unequipped. {idea}Allah sent Musa with what he needed before the hard part began.{/idea} Look at what you have already been given.
old: I am facing this with nothing in my hands.
new: When Allah sends me into something hard, He gives me what I need first.
try: List three things Allah has already given you for the hardest task in front of you.

title: Clear signs, and they called it magic.
subtitle: How you dismiss what you do not want
then: When the signs came to Pharaoh's people, {idea}clear and obvious{/idea}, they said it was magic. Ibn Kathir says they wanted to oppose it with their own magic, {trap}but they were defeated and sent back disgraced.{/trap}
now: Your friend points out something true about how you treat your sister. You reply: you are just being dramatic. {trap}A quick label lets you skip the hard truth.{/trap} The sign was clear. The label was a way out.
old: If I can name what is happening, I do not need to deal with it.
new: Giving a clear truth a dismissive label is a way of running from it.
try: Think of one piece of feedback you labelled and dismissed. Look at it again honestly.

title: They knew it was true, and said no.
subtitle: Denial out of pride, not doubt

row.title: pride
sub: I know, but I will not

then: Ibn Kathir says Pharaoh's people {trap}knew deep down that this was truth from Allah, but denied it, stubborn and arrogant.{/trap} They were too proud to follow. The Prophet ﷺ is told to see how they ended: drowned in a single morning.
now: You know you owe your colleague an apology. You know the habit is hurting you. You still argue, delay, change the subject. {trap}It is rarely about proof.{/trap} It is about not wanting to bend.
old: I just need more convincing before I change.
new: Sometimes I already know, and what stops me is pride, not doubt.
try: Do one thing today you already know is right but have been too proud to do.

title: Given knowledge, their first words were praise.
subtitle: How Dawud and Sulayman received a gift
then: Ibn Kathir says Allah gave Dawud and his son Sulayman {reward}power and authority in this world, and the position of Prophets.{/reward} Their reaction was praise. The surah introduction contrasts this with the Makkan chiefs, who had far less and were full of vanity.
now: You get the promotion. The exam result comes back high. The baby sleeps through the night. {idea}What comes out of your mouth first?{/idea} Dawud and Sulayman had far more and started with al-hamdu lillah.
old: When something good happens, it is mostly because I worked for it.
new: The first right response to any gift is to thank the One who gave it.
try: The next good news you get today, say al-hamdu lillah before telling anyone.

title: He inherited a mission, not a fortune.
subtitle: Sulayman, the birds, and evident bounty
then: Ibn Kathir explains Sulayman inherited {idea}kingship and prophethood, not wealth{/idea}, citing the Prophet ﷺ: "We Prophets cannot be inherited from; whatever we leave behind is charity." Sulayman understood birds and animals, and he called it {reward}clearly the blessings of Allah upon us.{/reward}
now: Your father left you a small shop, or a name people respect, or just his habit of praying at the masjid. {idea}The most valuable inheritance is rarely in the will.{/idea} And when you tell people what you have, the way you describe it shows who you credit.
old: What I inherit is measured by money and property.
new: The best inheritance is faith and responsibility, and every gift is Allah's bounty.
try: Name one good thing a parent or elder passed to you that is not money. Thank Allah for it.

title: A vast army, every one in its place.
subtitle: Sulayman's hosts of jinn, men and birds
then: Ibn Kathir describes Sulayman riding in a display of might, men behind him, then jinn, and {reward}birds shading him with their wings when it was hot.{/reward} Mujahid said officials kept each group in order {idea}so no one would step out of line.{/idea}
now: You lead a team, a household, a class, a WhatsApp group of cousins. The temptation is to act big. {idea}Real strength looks like order: everyone knows their place and no one gets lost.{/idea}
old: Having power means people notice me.
new: Power given by Allah is a trust to organize and look after people well.
try: Check on one person under your care today who might be falling out of line or left behind.

title: One small ant warned her whole valley.
subtitle: The ant who gave the surah its name

row.title: being crushed
sub: by those who do not notice

key.label: How she spoke of the army

then: The surah takes its name from this valley of the ants. As Sulayman's army crossed it, {idea}one ant called out to the others to go into their dwellings{/idea} so they would not be crushed. She added that Sulayman and his soldiers {idea}would not even perceive it.{/idea}
now: You see the scam message going around the family chat and you are the one who types: do not click this. {idea}One small voice can protect a whole group.{/idea} And you can warn without making anyone the villain.
old: I am too small for my warning to matter.
new: One small voice, used early and fairly, can save many.
try: Share one honest, useful warning with someone who needs it today, gently.

title: He smiled at an ant, then asked to be grateful.
subtitle: Sulayman's prayer for gratitude and good deeds
then: Sulayman understood the ant and {reward}smiled, amused.{/reward} Ibn Kathir explains his prayer: inspire me to give thanks for understanding the birds and animals, and for making my parents believers. Then {idea}join me with the righteous when I die.{/idea}
now: Your toddler says something funny, your colleague shares a small kindness. You smile. {idea}That smile is a door.{/idea} Sulayman turned his into a prayer to be grateful, to do good, and to end among good people.
old: Being grateful is something I can just decide to feel.
new: Even gratitude is a gift I ask Allah for, and it should include my parents.
try: Learn the first line of Sulayman's prayer, rabbi awzi'ni, and say it once tonight.

title: A king who noticed one missing bird.
subtitle: Sulayman checks on the hoopoe

row.title: is he absent?
sub: or do I not see him

then: Ibn Abbas and others said the hoopoe had a special skill: {reward}he could tell Sulayman where water lay under open land{/reward}, and how deep. One day Sulayman checked on the birds and could not see him. He first asked if the fault was in his own sight.
now: The quiet kid at the back of the class. The cousin who stopped showing up to Eid. The colleague who has gone silent on calls. {idea}Noticing who is missing is a kind of care.{/idea}
old: If someone drifts away, they will reach out if they need me.
new: Caring for people includes noticing who is not there.
try: Message one person you have not heard from in a while. Just ask how they are.

title: A firm warning, with an exception left open.
subtitle: Unless he brings a clear reason
then: Sulayman spoke strongly about the absent hoopoe, but added: {idea}unless he brings me a clear reason.{/idea} Sufyan bin Uyaynah and Abdullah bin Shaddad report that when the hoopoe returned and heard there was an exception, he said, {reward}then I am saved.{/reward}
now: Your teenager comes home two hours late. Your employee missed the deadline. {idea}You can be firm and still leave room for their reason.{/idea} That word unless is the difference between justice and anger.
old: When someone lets me down, I have every right to judge them straight away.
new: Being firm is fair only when I leave space to hear their reason.
try: Next time someone lets you down today, ask what happened before you react.

title: A small bird told a prophet something new.
subtitle: The hoopoe returns from Sheba
then: The hoopoe was not gone long. He told Sulayman: {idea}I have come to know something that you and your troops do not know.{/idea} Ibn Kathir says Saba refers to Himyar, a dynasty in Yemen, and the news was true and certain.
now: The intern spots the error in your slides. Your kid shows you how to fix the phone setting. {idea}Knowledge does not care about rank.{/idea} Sulayman, prophet and king, listened to a bird.
old: People below me have little to teach me.
new: The smallest person in the room may know exactly what I am missing.
try: Ask someone younger or junior to you for their view on something today, and listen.

title: A queen with everything and a great throne.
subtitle: The hoopoe describes the ruler of Sheba
then: Al-Hasan Al-Basri said this was Bilqis, queen of Saba. Ibn Kathir says she had {reward}all the conveniences a powerful monarch could need{/reward} and a throne adorned with gold, jewels and pearls. The surah introduction notes her wealth far exceeded that of the Quraysh.
now: You scroll past the house tours, the holiday photos, the big wedding. It looks like they have everything. {idea}Having everything still leaves the most important question open.{/idea} The next verse asks it.
old: People who have everything must have life figured out.
new: Wealth and power tell me what someone has, not where their heart is turned.
try: When you feel envy today, ask yourself what you would want more than their things.

title: Bowing to the sun instead of its Maker.
subtitle: The hoopoe sees the people of Sheba
then: Historians described her palace with windows the sun shone through as it rose and set, and {trap}the people prostrated to the sun morning and evening.{/trap} Ibn Kathir explains Shaytan made their deeds look good and kept them from the way of truth.
now: You do not bow to the sun. But what lights up your day? The salary, the likes, the approval of one person. {trap}Whatever you arrange your mornings and evenings around starts to act like a god.{/trap}
old: Worshipping things is something only ancient people did.
new: I can turn my whole day toward something bright that Allah made and forget Him.
try: Notice the first thing you reach for when you wake. Put a short dhikr before it tomorrow.

title: He brings out what is hidden, and knows yours.
subtitle: Why prostration belongs to Allah
then: The hoopoe explains why they should bow to Allah. Ibn Abbas said He {idea}knows everything hidden in the heavens and the earth.{/idea} Ibn Kathir adds He knows what His servants say and do in secret and in the open, both the same to Him.
now: Your search history. The message you deleted. The thought you had during the meeting. The quiet good you did that nobody saw. {idea}All of it is open to Him.{/idea} That is a warning and a comfort at once.
old: What I do in private stays private.
new: Allah knows my hidden side, both the faults and the quiet good.
try: Do one good deed today that no one will ever know about.

title: Her throne was great. His Throne is greater.
subtitle: The hoopoe ends with tawhid
then: The hoopoe had just described the queen's great throne. Now he says Allah is {idea}Lord of the Supreme Throne, and there is none greater than Him in all of creation.{/idea} Ibn Kathir notes the hoopoe was calling to good, and cites a hadith in which the Prophet ﷺ forbade killing hoopoes.
now: The CEO's office. The mansion on the hill. The stage at the conference. {idea}They feel huge when you stand in front of them.{/idea} Next to the Lord of the Great Throne, every earthly throne is small.
old: Powerful people and big institutions are the biggest things in my world.
new: Every throne I am impressed by is tiny next to the Throne of Allah.
try: Before a meeting or call that intimidates you, say la ilaha illa Allah once, slowly.

title: Good news or not, check it first.
subtitle: Sulayman tests the hoopoe's report
then: Sulayman did not dismiss the hoopoe or accept him blindly. Ibn Kathir explains he wondered whether the bird was telling the truth, or {trap}lying to save himself from the threat.{/trap} So he said: {idea}we shall see.{/idea}
now: A screenshot lands in the family group: shocking news about someone you know. Your thumb is already on forward. {idea}We will see is a powerful sentence.{/idea} Check it before you pass it on.
old: If news comes from someone I trust, I can share it straight away.
new: Even trusted sources get checked before I act on what they say.
try: Before forwarding the next message today, check whether it is true.

title: Deliver the letter, step back, and watch.
subtitle: Sulayman sends the hoopoe to Sheba
then: Sulayman wrote a letter and told the hoopoe to deliver it and draw back. Ibn Kathir says the bird threw it through a small window into her chamber, then {idea}stepped to one side out of good manners{/idea} to see what they would do.
now: You finally send the honest email to your brother, or share the reminder with a friend. Then you refresh every two minutes. {idea}Deliver it well, then step back.{/idea} Give them room to answer.
old: After I say something important, I have to keep pushing until they respond.
new: My job is to deliver the message with good manners, then give space.
try: Send one message you have been holding back, then put your phone away for an hour.

title: She called it a noble letter.
subtitle: Bilqis gathers her chiefs
then: Bilqis was amazed and confused when the letter landed in her chamber. Ibn Kathir says she called it noble {idea}because of the wondrous way it came: a bird delivered it, then stood aside out of good manners.{/idea} She gathered her commanders, ministers and leaders.
now: A message arrives that could hurt your pride: a note from your landlord, a hard email from your manager. {idea}You can see what is honorable in it before you react.{/idea} Bilqis did not tear it up. She called people in to think.
old: A message that challenges me is an attack to push back on.
new: A challenging message can be noble, and deserves to be read with care.
try: Reread one hard message you received recently, looking for what is fair in it.

title: The letter began with the name of the Merciful.
subtitle: How a prophet opened a hard message
then: The queen read the letter aloud. It named its sender, Sulayman, and began {idea}In the Name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.{/idea} Ibn Kathir says they knew then it was from Allah's Prophet and that {trap}they could not match him.{/trap}
now: You are about to write the difficult text: to an ex, to a sibling you fell out with, to the client who has not paid. {idea}What you put first sets the tone.{/idea} Sulayman, with all his power, opened with mercy.
old: When I have the upper hand, I can lead with strength.
new: Even a firm message starts best with Allah's name and His mercy.
try: Say Bismillah before the next hard message you write today, and let it soften one word.

title: Do not be arrogant. Come in submission.
subtitle: A short letter, straight to the point
then: Ibn Kathir says the letter was {idea}the utmost in brevity and eloquence, coming straight to the point.{/idea} Qatadah explained: do not be arrogant with me. Abdur-Rahman bin Zayd said: {trap}do not refuse or be too arrogant to come.{/trap}
now: You write five paragraphs to say one thing, and the point gets lost. {idea}Two clear lines can do more than a long speech.{/idea} And the heart of the matter is often the same: let go of pride and come back.
old: Important things need long explanations.
new: The clearest call is short: drop the pride and turn to Allah.
try: Rewrite one message you need to send in two sentences.

title: A queen who would not decide alone.
subtitle: Bilqis asks her chiefs for advice
then: After reading Sulayman's letter, Bilqis consulted her leaders. She said she would {idea}decide no case until they came together and offered their advice.{/idea} The surah introduction describes her as a ruler of a wealthy people who still did not act from vanity.
now: The big decision: moving cities, a new job, a marriage proposal. {idea}You do not have to decide it alone in your head at 2am.{/idea} Call the people whose judgment you trust and ask.
old: Asking for advice makes me look weak or unsure.
new: Even someone with full authority is wiser when she listens first.
try: Ask one trusted person for their honest view on a decision you are facing.

title: We are strong, they said, but you decide.
subtitle: The chiefs offer force, then defer
then: Ibn Kathir explains the chiefs {trap}reminded her of their great numbers, preparedness and strength{/trap}, then handed the decision back. Their words: {idea}we have the power if you want to fight, but the matter is yours to decide.{/idea}
now: Your friends are ready to fight your battle: we will tell him off, we will post about it. {trap}Being able to hit back is not a reason to.{/trap} The best advice leaves room for you to think it over.
old: If I have the strength to win a fight, I should use it.
new: Strength is a tool, and the wiser question is what will actually help.
try: In one disagreement today, choose not to use an advantage you have.

title: She knew what conquering kings leave behind.
subtitle: Bilqis weighs the cost of war
then: Ibn Abbas explained that Bilqis said kings {trap}destroy a town they enter and make its most honorable people the lowest.{/trap} Then Allah said: {idea}and thus they do{/idea}, confirming her words. She saw where a fight would lead.
now: You picture winning the argument with your spouse, the lawsuit with your neighbor. {trap}Winning can still wreck the house.{/trap} Bilqis looked past the victory to what it would leave behind.
old: Winning a conflict is the same as coming out well.
new: Before any fight, I should picture what it will do to the people around me.
try: Before your next argument, ask what the relationship will look like afterward.

title: She chose a gift and patience over a fight.
subtitle: Testing whether he was a king or a prophet
then: Bilqis turned to {idea}peaceful means, seeking a truce.{/idea} Qatadah praised her wisdom: she understood how gift-giving has a good effect on people. Ibn Abbas and others said she reasoned: {idea}if he accepts it he is a king; if not, he is a Prophet, so follow him.{/idea}
now: The tension with your in-laws is building. You could text something sharp, or you could bring dessert on Friday and see. {reward}A gift and a pause can tell you more than a fight.{/reward}
old: When someone pressures me, I must either fight or give in.
new: A gift and patience can lower tension and reveal what someone really wants.
try: Give a small gift to someone you are tense with this week.

title: What Allah gave me is better than your gift.
subtitle: Sulayman refuses to be bought
then: Scholars said she sent {reward}a huge gift of gold, jewels and pearls.{/reward} Ibn Kathir says Sulayman did not even look at it. He asked if they were trying {trap}to flatter him with wealth so he would leave them with their shirk{/trap}, and said what Allah gave him was better.
now: Someone offers you a bonus to look the other way. A friend's family offers money so you will drop a complaint. {idea}When you are content with what Allah gave you, you cannot be bought.{/idea}
old: If the offer is big enough, it is fine to bend a little.
new: What Allah has given me is enough, so no gift should buy my silence about what is right.
try: Name one thing someone could offer you to compromise. Decide now that it is not for sale.

title: Send the gift back. The message stands.
subtitle: A firm reply that led to her submission
then: Sulayman sent the envoys back with their gift and a firm warning. Ibn Kathir says when they reported it, {reward}she and her people paid heed and came to him in humility, intending to follow him in Islam.{/reward} When Sulayman realized they were coming, {reward}he rejoiced greatly.{/reward}
now: You returned the expensive present because it came with strings. It felt harsh. {idea}A clear no can be what finally lets the other person take you seriously.{/idea} The goal is not to win but to see them come round.
old: Refusing a gift will only make things worse.
new: A firm, clear no can open the door, and the hope behind it is the other person's good.
try: Give one clear, kind no today that you have been avoiding.

title: Who can bring her throne before she arrives?
subtitle: Sulayman prepares a sign for the queen
then: Yazid bin Ruman reported that Bilqis said she knew he was more than a king. She locked her throne in the innermost of seven rooms and set out. Ibn Kathir says Sulayman wanted it brought {idea}to furnish proof of his prophethood before Bilqis and her people.{/idea}
now: Your cousin is coming to visit, curious but unsure about faith. {idea}What you prepare before they arrive matters.{/idea} Not to impress them with yourself, but to help them see something true.
old: When I want someone to take my faith seriously, I should talk more.
new: I can prepare signs ahead of time, through how I live, that point beyond me.
try: Before seeing someone today, plan one kind act that reflects your faith without words.

title: Strong and trustworthy, but not fast enough.
subtitle: The Ifrit's offer
then: Mujahid said the Ifrit was a giant jinn. He offered to bring the throne before Sulayman rose from his sitting, which As-Suddi said lasted until noon. Ibn Abbas explained his claim: {idea}strong enough to carry it and trustworthy with the jewels it contains.{/idea}
now: You are hiring someone, or choosing who to leave your kids with. Skill is half of it. {idea}Can they carry it, and will they keep it safe?{/idea} You want to be both of those for the people who depend on you.
old: Being good at the job is all that counts.
new: Real competence is strength and trustworthiness together.
try: Do one task today with both full effort and complete honesty.

title: The throne arrived, and he called it a test.
subtitle: Gratitude benefits the grateful
then: Ibn Abbas said the man was Asif, Sulayman's scribe. He prayed, and the throne appeared in a blink. Sulayman said {idea}this is by the grace of my Lord, to test whether I am grateful.{/idea} Ibn Kathir adds: Allah has no need of anyone's worship, and gratitude is for the grateful.
now: The thing you prayed for arrives faster than you hoped: the visa, the test result, the offer letter. {idea}That moment is the exam, not the reward.{/idea} Do you say al-hamdu lillah, or just move on to the next thing?
old: When I get what I asked for, the test is over.
new: Getting what I wanted is itself the test, and thanks helps me, not Allah.
try: Recall the last prayer that was answered. Thank Allah for it specifically today.

title: Change her throne a little and see.
subtitle: A test of her judgment
then: Sulayman ordered the throne altered. Mujahid said red was made yellow and green made red. Ibn Kathir explains it was to see {idea}whether she recognized it and how composed she would be{/idea}, and whether she would be guided.
now: Life rearranges the familiar: a parent ages, a job changes shape, your city looks different. {idea}Can you still see clearly when things are rearranged?{/idea} That is often the real test.
old: Tests are about catching me out.
new: Many tests are about whether I see clearly when the familiar looks different.
try: Look at one changed situation in your life and name what is still the same underneath.

title: As though it were the very same.
subtitle: Her careful answer about the throne
then: Ibn Kathir calls her {idea}wise and steadfast, intelligent and strong-willed.{/idea} She did not rush to say yes, since her throne was far away, nor no, since it resembled hers. Her answer was {idea}the ultimate in intelligence and resolve.{/idea} Mujahid said Sulayman then spoke of the knowledge given to them.
now: Someone asks you about a rumor, a diagnosis, a story you only half know. You feel pressure to be sure. {idea}Saying exactly what you know, no more, no less, is a skill.{/idea}
old: I need to give a firm yes or no to look smart.
new: An honest answer can be careful and match exactly what I know.
try: Today, when unsure, say "I think so, but I am not certain" instead of guessing.

title: Her old worship was what held her back.
subtitle: What stood between Bilqis and the truth
then: Mujahid and Sa'id bin Jubayr read this as Sulayman's words: {trap}what stopped her from worshipping Allah alone was what she used to worship{/trap}, because she came from a disbelieving people. Ibn Kathir notes she declared her Islam soon after.
now: You are smart, educated, thoughtful. And still some habits stick because "this is how our family does it." {trap}Brilliance does not free you from what you grew up around.{/trap} Noticing it is the first step.
old: Clever people are not held back by habits they inherited.
new: Even a sharp mind can be held back by what it was raised to bow to.
try: Name one habit you keep only because your surroundings do. Ask if it pleases Allah.

title: I wronged myself, and I submit with Sulayman.
subtitle: The glass floor and her turning

row.title: I submit
sub: to the Lord of the worlds

then: Sulayman had a palace of smooth glass built over flowing water. Bilqis thought it was water. Ibn Kathir says when she saw what Allah had given him, {reward}she submitted and said she had wronged herself{/reward} by worshipping the sun, and she submitted {idea}together with Sulayman to Allah.{/idea}
now: You spent years sure you had something figured out, then one moment shows you were wrong. {reward}"I wronged myself" is not defeat.{/reward} And you do not turn to a person. You stand beside them, before Allah.
old: Admitting I was wrong means losing to someone.
new: Admitting I wronged myself is how I join others in turning to Allah.
try: Say "I was wrong about this" to Allah, out loud, about one thing today.

title: One call, and the town split in two.
subtitle: Salih is sent to Thamud
then: Allah sent Salih to Thamud, {idea}one of their own{/idea}, calling them to worship Allah alone. Mujahid said they became two parties: {trap}believers and disbelievers{/trap}, quarreling with each other. Ibn Kathir links it to the arrogant leaders mocking the weak who believed.
now: You start praying at work, or stop joining the gossip at lunch. Suddenly there are two groups at the table. {idea}You did not make the split. You made the choice visible.{/idea} Stay kind with both sides.
old: If doing right causes friction, I must be doing something wrong.
new: A clear call to good will sometimes show where people already stand.
try: Keep one good practice today even if it makes you stand out, and stay gentle about it.

title: Why rush toward harm instead of good?
subtitle: Salih asks his people to seek forgiveness
then: Ibn Kathir explains Salih's question: {trap}why are you praying for the punishment to come{/trap}, and not asking Allah for His mercy? He urged them to {reward}seek forgiveness so they might receive mercy.{/reward}
now: Your doctor warns about your blood pressure and you joke: something has to get me eventually. {trap}Daring the warning feels brave.{/trap} The wiser move is quieter: ask for help and change course while the door is open.
old: If the warning is real, let it happen and we will see.
new: When I am warned, the smart response is to seek forgiveness, not to dare the consequence.
try: Say astaghfirullah three times today, thinking of one specific thing.

title: They blamed him for their bad luck.
subtitle: Calling the messenger a bad omen

key.label: Where the bad luck comes from

then: Ibn Kathir says {trap}whenever anything bad happened to them, they said it was because of Salih and his companions.{/trap} Salih answered that their fate was with Allah. Qatadah explained: {idea}you are being tested to see whether you will obey or disobey.{/idea}
now: The car breaks down the week your new colleague starts. The house feels unlucky since your sister-in-law moved in. {trap}It is easy to make a person the reason.{/trap} The question is how you respond to the test.
old: When things go wrong, someone must be bringing bad luck.
new: Hard times are tests from Allah, not proof that someone is cursed.
try: Catch one moment today when you blame a person for bad luck. Replace it with a dua.

title: Nine men spread corruption and never set things right.
subtitle: The ringleaders of Thamud
then: Ibn Kathir says these nine {trap}forced their opinions on the people because they were the leaders.{/trap} Ibn Abbas said they instigated the killing of the she-camel. Ata said {trap}they used to break silver coins{/trap}, and Sa'id bin Al-Musayyib called cutting coins part of spreading corruption.
now: Shaving a few minutes off timesheets. Short-changing a customer by a coin. Pushing your opinion on the whole family because you are the eldest. {trap}Corruption often starts small and from the top.{/trap}
old: Corruption is what powerful people do on the news.
new: Corruption includes the small cheats and the pressure I put on people below me.
try: Fix one small unfairness you have been letting slide, even if no one would notice.

title: They swore by Allah to commit a crime.
subtitle: The night plot against Salih
then: Ibn Kathir explains they plotted to kill Salih and his family at night, then tell his relatives {trap}they knew nothing, and that they were telling the truth because none of them had seen anything.{/trap} They sealed it with an oath by Allah.
now: "I never said that" when you typed it. "I did not take it" when you let someone else do it. {trap}Wording a lie to sound true still makes it a lie.{/trap} Allah knows what you planned.
old: If my words are technically true, I am not lying.
new: A clever wording does not hide the truth of what I did from Allah.
try: Notice one time today you are tempted to give a technically true answer. Give the honest one.

title: They planned, and Allah planned.
subtitle: The plot they could not see coming
then: Ibn Abi Hatim reports they waited in a cave near Salih's place of prayer to kill him. {idea}A rock came down from the mountain and covered the cave's mouth{/idea} with them inside. {reward}Allah saved Salih and those with him.{/reward}
now: Someone at work is quietly building a case against you. Your ex is spreading stories. It keeps you up at night. {idea}Their plan is not the last plan.{/idea} Do what is right, and trust the One who sees everything.
old: If people are plotting against me, I have to out-plot them.
new: Allah has a plan above every plan, and they do not see it coming.
try: Hand one worry about someone's scheming to Allah in dua tonight, then sleep.

title: Look how their plotting ended.
subtitle: The outcome of the plan against Salih
then: Mujahid said {trap}before they could reach Salih, they and their people were all destroyed.{/trap} Ibn Kathir says Allah punished some of them in one place and some in another. The verse asks the listener to look at how it ended.
now: You have watched someone build their success on lies and lose it all. {idea}The verse asks you to look, not to gloat.{/idea} Ask where your own plans are headed.
old: Stories of ruined people are about someone else.
new: Every ending I see is a mirror for checking where my own plans lead.
try: Look at one plan you are working on. Ask how it ends if you keep going this way.

title: Empty houses that still speak.
subtitle: The ruins of Thamud as a sign
then: Their houses were left {trap}in utter ruin, deserted, because they did wrong.{/trap} The verse says this is {idea}a sign for people who know.{/idea} The listeners in Makkah knew the old ruins of Thamud.
now: You walk past a shop that closed, a once-grand house now empty. {idea}Every abandoned place says: nothing here is permanent.{/idea} People who know take the lesson home with them.
old: Ruins are just old buildings.
new: Empty places remind me that only what I do for Allah lasts.
try: The next empty or abandoned building you pass, say a short dua for a good ending.

title: Those who believed and were mindful were saved.
subtitle: The rescue inside the story
then: After the ruin, the verse turns: {reward}Allah saved those who believed and had taqwa.{/reward} Ibn Kathir notes the believers had been called a bad omen and were the weaker party. They were the ones who came through.
now: You feel outnumbered: the only one in your office who prays, the one parent who sets screen limits. {reward}Being few is not the same as being lost.{/reward} Faith and mindfulness are what carry you through.
old: If I am in the minority, I am on the losing side.
new: Safety comes from faith and mindfulness of Allah, not from numbers.
try: Thank Allah today for one person who shares your faith and helps you keep it.

title: Doing wrong openly, with eyes wide open.
subtitle: Lut confronts his people
then: Lut warned his people of Allah's punishment. Ibn Kathir explains {trap}while you see{/trap} as {trap}while you see one another, practicing every kind of evil in your meetings.{/trap} They knew what they were doing, and did it openly.
now: The group chat where everyone shares what should not be shared. The office joke no one stops. {trap}When wrong becomes normal in the room, it gets harder to see.{/trap} Notice where you have stopped noticing.
old: If everyone around me does it openly, it cannot be that bad.
new: Doing wrong openly, with full knowledge, is a sign the heart has gone numb.
try: Leave or quietly change one gathering, chat or habit where wrong has become normal.

title: Desire leading where knowledge said no.
subtitle: Lut calls his people ignorant
then: Lut said they were a people who behave senselessly. Ibn Kathir explains: {trap}you do not know anything of what is natural or what is prescribed by Allah.{/trap} He links it to their leaving what Allah had created for them.
now: Late at night, you know what you should close, delete, or walk away from. {trap}Desire talks louder than what you know.{/trap} The verse calls that ignorance, even when you know better.
old: My desires are just part of me, so following them is natural.
new: Letting desire overrule what Allah taught me is a kind of ignorance.
try: Next time a desire pushes against what you know is right, wait five minutes before acting.

title: Their only answer: throw out the clean ones.
subtitle: Purity treated as a crime
then: They gave no other answer. Ibn Kathir explains their thinking: {trap}these people feel embarrassed by your deeds and do not approve, so expel them.{/trap} Lut's family was accused of one thing: {idea}wanting to stay pure.{/idea}
now: Your friends tease you for not drinking at the party, for leaving early, for not joining the gossip. "You think you are better than us." {idea}Sometimes your example is the whole argument.{/idea}
old: If people push me out for my standards, I must be doing something wrong.
new: Being pushed away for staying clean can be a sign I am holding on to something good.
try: Keep one standard today that others tease you for, and smile when they do.

title: Saved, except the one who helped the wrong.
subtitle: Lut's wife remained behind
then: Ibn Kathir says Lut's wife was destroyed with her people {trap}because she was a helper to what they did and approved of their evil deeds.{/trap} She told them about Lut's guests. Being married to a prophet did not save her.
now: You did not write the cruel post, you just liked it. You did not cheat, you just told him where the answers were. {trap}Helping and approving are their own deeds.{/trap} And who you are close to will not carry you.
old: If I did not commit the wrong myself, I am not involved.
new: Helping or approving of wrong counts, and being close to good people will not save me alone.
try: Undo one small way you have been helping or cheering on something wrong.

title: They were warned, and still went ahead.
subtitle: The end of Lut's people
then: Ibn Kathir says the rain was stones, one after another. It fell on {trap}those against whom proof was established and whom the warning reached{/trap}, yet they denied the Messenger and resolved to drive him out.
now: You have heard the reminder at Jumuah, read the verse, been told kindly by a friend. {idea}Hearing the warning is a mercy.{/idea} It is still not too late to act on it today.
old: I have heard all the warnings before, so they do not apply to me anymore.
new: Every warning I have heard is a mercy and a responsibility while I still have time.
try: Think of one reminder you keep hearing and ignoring. Take one small step on it today.

title: Praise Allah, greet His chosen, then ask the question.
subtitle: How the second half of the surah opens
then: The Prophet ﷺ is told to {idea}praise Allah for His innumerable blessings{/idea} and send peace on His chosen servants. Abdur-Rahman bin Zayd said these are the Prophets; Ath-Thawri and As-Suddi said the Companions, and Ibn Kathir says both fit. Then comes the question: {trap}is Allah better, or what they set up beside Him?{/trap}
now: Before you argue with anyone about faith, start like this: thank Allah, pray for the good people who came before you. {idea}Then ask yourself the question first.{/idea} What do you actually lean on when things get hard?
old: Talking about Allah starts with proving people wrong.
new: It starts with praise and peace, and then an honest question about what I rely on.
try: Before your next prayer, say al-hamdu lillah and send peace on the Prophet ﷺ.

title: You plant the seed. Can you make the tree grow?
subtitle: Gardens of beauty from rain
then: Ibn Kathir says the idolators of Makkah {idea}admitted Allah created everything and sends the rain{/idea}, yet worshipped others who they admitted could create nothing. The verse asks: is there a god with Allah? The answer: {trap}they set up equals to Him.{/trap}
now: You water the tomato plant on your balcony every evening. One morning there is fruit. {idea}You did your part, but you did not make it grow.{/idea} Same with your career, your kids, your savings.
old: What I worked for, I produced.
new: I plant and water, and Allah is the one who makes anything grow.
try: Look at one plant or tree today and say subhanAllah for what you did not make.

title: Stable ground under your feet is a gift.
subtitle: Earth, rivers, mountains, and a barrier
then: Ibn Kathir explains the earth is made {reward}smooth and calm by His grace{/reward}, since a shaking earth would be no place to live. Rivers flow where people need them, and a barrier keeps sweet and salt water apart so each stays as it is meant to be. Yet {trap}most of them do not know.{/trap}
now: You fall asleep in an apartment building. You fill a glass from the tap. You never think the floor might move. {idea}Every quiet, ordinary day is resting on something He arranged.{/idea}
old: Solid ground and clean water are just how the world is.
new: The ground that holds still and the water I drink are daily mercies from Allah.
try: Drink your next glass of water slowly and thank Allah for it before you swallow.

title: Who answers you when you are desperate?
subtitle: The One the distressed call on
then: Ibn Kathir says Allah is {idea}the One people call on in difficulty and turn to when calamity strikes.{/idea} He cites the Prophet ﷺ telling a man he called people to Allah, who relieves harm and returns the lost. The verse ends: {trap}little do you remember.{/trap}
now: The hospital corridor at 3am. The phone call you cannot believe. You pray like never before. {idea}He answers the desperate.{/idea} The test is whether you still remember Him a month later, when it is all fine.
old: I will pray hard when something serious happens.
new: The One who answered me in my worst moment deserves my remembrance on ordinary days too.
try: Remember one hard time Allah got you through. Thank Him for it today.

title: Guided through darkness, rain announced by wind.
subtitle: Signposts and good news in nature
then: Ibn Kathir explains that Allah guides people {idea}by the heavenly and earthly signposts He created{/idea}, like the stars. He sends winds ahead of the rain clouds, {reward}His mercy to servants suffering drought and despair.{/reward}
now: Driving home late on a dark road, the map app finds your way. The cool wind before a storm after a heatwave. {idea}Every way through darkness was set up by Him.{/idea}
old: Finding my way is just technology and skill.
new: Every light that guides me through the dark, and every hint of relief, comes from Allah.
try: The next time you feel a breeze, say al-hamdu lillah for His mercy.

title: He started creation and will do it again.
subtitle: Show your proof, if you have any
then: Ibn Kathir says Allah {idea}originates creation by His might and then repeats it.{/idea} Rain goes into the earth, comes out as springs, and brings crops and flowers. The listeners are told to produce proof for other gods, but {trap}they have no proof or evidence.{/trap}
now: You look at an ultrasound, a tiny heartbeat on a screen. {idea}The One who did this once can do it again.{/idea} If He began you, bringing you back is not hard for Him.
old: Coming back to life after death is hard to imagine.
new: The One who created me the first time can easily do it again.
try: Look at a photo of yourself as a baby and reflect on who made you.

title: Only Allah knows the unseen.
subtitle: No one knows when the Hour comes

key.label: Who to ask about the future

then: Ibn Kathir calls this {idea}an absolute exception{/idea}: no one besides Allah knows the unseen. He cites the hadith where the Prophet ﷺ told Jibril about the Hour: {idea}the one being asked does not know more than the one asking.{/idea}
now: The horoscope app. The friend who "just knows" how things will turn out. Your own anxious mind running every scenario. {idea}None of them hold the keys.{/idea} You can let go of needing to know.
old: If I could just know what is coming, I would feel safe.
new: Only Allah knows what is coming, so I can rest in trusting Him.
try: When you catch yourself worrying about the future today, say "Allah knows" and breathe.

title: Their knowledge stopped short, then doubt, then blindness.
subtitle: Three steps away from the Hereafter
then: Ibn Kathir explains their {trap}knowledge and amazement stopped short of knowing its time{/trap}, and that the disbelievers {trap}doubt it will come to pass{/trap}. Finally they are {trap}blind and completely ignorant about it.{/trap}
now: You know a lot about your industry, your favorite team, the latest phones. Ask about the Hereafter and it gets vague. {trap}Not thinking about it turns into doubting it.{/trap} Doubt left alone becomes not seeing at all.
old: I will think about the afterlife properly when I am older.
new: Leaving the Hereafter unexamined slowly turns into doubt and then blindness.
try: Spend five minutes today reading or listening to something about the Hereafter.

title: Dust and bones, they asked, brought back?
subtitle: The doubt about resurrection
then: Ibn Kathir says the idolators denied the Resurrection, {trap}considering it extremely unlikely that bodies will be re-created after they have become bones and dust.{/trap} The verse before had just said He begins creation and repeats it.
now: You stand at a grave on a cold morning, the earth freshly turned over someone you loved. It feels final. {idea}The verse answers that feeling.{/idea} Dust is not the end of the story for the One who made you from it.
old: Once someone is buried, that is the end.
new: Dust is not too far gone for the One who created from nothing.
try: Make dua today for someone you have lost, by name.

title: We have heard this forever, they said. Old stories.
subtitle: When familiarity breeds dismissal
then: Ibn Kathir explains their words: {trap}we and our forefathers have been hearing this for a long time, but we have never seen it happen.{/trap} They called it tales passed down from old books, with no basis in reality.
now: You have heard about death and judgment since you were a kid in Quran class. {trap}It has become background noise.{/trap} Hearing something often does not make it less true.
old: I have heard this all my life, so it feels like old stories.
new: A truth I have heard many times is still true, and still coming.
try: Read one verse about the Hereafter today as if hearing it for the first time.

title: Go and look at how it ended for them.
subtitle: History as evidence
then: Ibn Kathir says the Prophet ﷺ was told to answer them this way: look at {trap}how the punishment struck those who denied the Messengers{/trap} and how {reward}Allah saved the Messengers and the believers who followed them.{/reward} That itself shows the Message is true.
now: You visit old ruins on holiday, or read about a family empire that collapsed. {idea}Do not just take the photo.{/idea} Ask what they relied on, and how it ended.
old: History is a list of old facts.
new: The endings of past people are evidence I am meant to look at and learn from.
try: On your next trip or history read, find one lesson about how something ended.

title: Do not grieve over them or be crushed by plots.
subtitle: Comfort for the Prophet ﷺ
then: Ibn Kathir explains this was {idea}to comfort the Prophet ﷺ{/idea}: do not feel sorry for them or {trap}kill yourself with regret{/trap}, and do not be distressed by their plotting, because {reward}Allah will help and support you.{/reward}
now: Your brother will not listen. Your friend keeps making the same bad choice. You lie awake replaying it. {idea}Care, advise, pray, and then let Allah carry what you cannot.{/idea}
old: If someone I love rejects good advice, it is my failure.
new: I can grieve for people without being crushed, because their choices and my support belong to Allah.
try: Make dua for one person you are worried about, then consciously hand it to Allah.

title: So when is it coming, they mocked.
subtitle: Asking for a date to avoid the question
then: Ibn Kathir says the idolators asked about the Day of Resurrection {trap}but thought it unlikely that it would ever come to pass.{/trap} The question was not curiosity. It was a challenge: if it is real, give us a date.
now: "Everyone has been saying the end is near for centuries." You hear it at the dinner table, or you think it yourself. {idea}The date is not yours to know.{/idea} Your readiness is.
old: Without a date, I do not need to think about it seriously.
new: Not knowing when is the very reason to be ready now.
try: Ask yourself honestly: if it were tomorrow, what one thing would I fix today? Fix it.

title: What you rush toward may already be behind you.
subtitle: Closer than you think
then: Ibn Abbas said: {trap}that which you wish to hasten on has come close to you, or some of it has.{/trap} Mujahid, Qatadah and As-Suddi held the same view. The Prophet ﷺ was told to answer the mocking question with this.
now: You keep saying you will sort your prayers out after the wedding, after the move, after the kids grow. {trap}The end is not waiting for your schedule.{/trap} It might be one step behind you.
old: I have plenty of time to get ready.
new: What I keep postponing may be much closer than I think.
try: Do one thing today that you have been saving for "later" in your faith.

title: Full of grace to people, thanked by few.
subtitle: Why the punishment has not come yet
then: Right after the deniers asked when the punishment would come, Allah says He is full of grace to mankind. Ibn Kathir explains {reward}He abundantly bestows His blessings on them even though they wrong themselves{/reward}, and still {trap}they do not give thanks, except a few.{/trap}
now: You skipped Fajr again, snapped at your mother, and still woke up healthy, with coffee and a paycheck coming. {reward}The blessings did not stop.{/reward} That is not proof nothing matters. It is grace giving you room.
old: If nothing bad happens when I mess up, it must not matter.
new: The good that keeps coming despite my faults is grace, and it deserves thanks.
try: Write down three blessings you received today despite something you did wrong.

title: He knows what your chest hides and what you say.
subtitle: No gap between the hidden and the shown
then: Ibn Kathir explains {idea}He knows what is hidden in their hearts just as He knows what is easily visible.{/idea} He cites verses saying it is the same to Him whether speech is hidden or open, and that He knows the secret and what is even more hidden.
now: You smile in the meeting while resenting your manager. You post the Ramadan quote while holding a grudge. {idea}He sees the chest and the caption.{/idea} You can stop working so hard on two versions of yourself.
old: What I feel inside is my business, as long as I act fine.
new: Allah sees my inner state as clearly as my actions, so I can work on both honestly.
try: Pick one feeling you hide behind a smile. Tell Allah about it in your own words.

title: Nothing hidden anywhere is missing from the Record.
subtitle: All of it written in a clear Book
then: Ibn Abbas said {idea}there is nothing in the heaven and the earth but it is in a Clear Book.{/idea} Ibn Kathir links it to the verse saying Allah knows all that is in the heavens and earth, it is all in the Book, and that is easy for Him.
now: The sadaqah you gave years ago that you forgot about. The tears no one saw. The small cruelty you hoped would fade. {idea}None of it fell through the cracks.{/idea} That is comfort and caution together.
old: Small things I did long ago are gone and forgotten.
new: Every hidden thing is written, so no good I do is wasted and no wrong is lost.
try: Do one small good deed today knowing it will be written, even if you forget it.

title: The Quran settles what people argued over.
subtitle: A moderate word of truth
then: Ibn Kathir says the Quran narrates the truth about matters the Children of Israel differed on, {idea}such as their different opinions about Isa.{/idea} It came with {idea}the moderate word of truth and justice{/idea}: that he was a servant of Allah and one of His noble Prophets.
now: The family argument about an uncle who either did everything wrong or could do no wrong. The online fight where every side is extreme. {idea}Truth is often the just middle.{/idea} You can look for it instead of picking a camp.
old: In any argument, I have to pick the side that sounds strongest.
new: The truth is often balanced, and I can look for the just word between extremes.
try: In one disagreement today, say something fair about both sides before giving your view.

title: For the believers, a guide and a mercy.
subtitle: What the Quran does in a heart
then: After settling old disagreements, the verse says the Quran is {idea}guidance for the hearts of those who believe in it{/idea}, and {reward}a mercy to them.{/reward} The surah opened the same way: guidance and good news for the believers.
now: It is a heavy night. You open the Quran not to study, just because nothing else helps. {reward}One verse lands exactly where it hurts.{/reward} That is the mercy part.
old: The Quran is mostly a list of rules.
new: The Quran is guidance and a mercy, something my heart can lean on.
try: Tonight, read a few verses slowly when you feel low, just for comfort.

title: Your Lord will judge between them.
subtitle: Some arguments are settled on the Day
then: Ibn Kathir explains Allah will decide between them {idea}on the Day of Resurrection{/idea}. He is All-Mighty and {idea}All-Knowing, knowing all that His servants do and say.{/idea}
now: The inheritance dispute that never resolved. The friend who still tells the story wrong. {idea}Not every argument needs to be won this week.{/idea} Some you can leave with the One who knows everything.
old: If I do not win this argument now, injustice wins.
new: Allah will judge every dispute fairly, so I do not have to settle all of them myself.
try: Choose one old argument and let it go to Allah, out loud, today.

title: Rely on Allah. You are on clear truth.
subtitle: Steadiness when opposed
then: Ibn Kathir says the Prophet ﷺ was told to {idea}put his trust in Allah in all his affairs and convey the Message{/idea}, because he was following manifest truth, even though opposed by those who opposed him.
now: You are the only one in the family keeping halal income, or the one who will not cut corners at work. People push back. {reward}Being opposed does not make you wrong.{/reward} Lean on Allah and keep going.
old: When many people push back, I should probably give in.
new: If I am on the truth, I can rely on Allah and stay steady.
try: Say hasbunallahu wa ni'mal wakil before facing someone who opposes what is right.

title: You cannot make someone hear who turns away.
subtitle: The limits of a messenger
then: Ibn Kathir explains the Prophet ﷺ {trap}cannot cause them to hear anything that will benefit them{/trap}, like those whose hearts are veiled and whose ears are deaf. The verse pictures people {trap}turning their backs and fleeing{/trap} from the call.
now: You have explained it to your friend five different ways. You sent the article, the lecture, the gentle text. {idea}Some people are walking away while you talk.{/idea} That is not your failure.
old: If someone does not listen, I have not explained it well enough.
new: My job is to speak well; making someone hear belongs to Allah.
try: Stop pushing one conversation that is not landing. Make dua for that person instead.

title: Only those who believe will truly listen.
subtitle: Who the message reaches
then: Ibn Kathir says {reward}those who have hearing and insight will respond{/reward}: those whose hearing and sight benefit their hearts, and who are {idea}humble towards Allah and the Message.{/idea}
now: You have heard the same khutbah topic ten times. One Friday, it suddenly hits. {idea}What changed was not the words. It was your heart.{/idea} Hearing well begins with being humble.
old: I have heard this before, so I already know it.
new: Real hearing comes from a humble heart, not from having heard it before.
try: At the next reminder you hear, ask Allah first to open your heart to it.

title: A creature from the earth will speak.
subtitle: A sign near the end of time
then: Ibn Kathir says this beast will emerge at the end of time, {trap}when mankind has become corrupt and neglected the commands of Allah.{/trap} He cites the hadith in Muslim: {idea}hasten to do good deeds before six things appear{/idea}, including the beast.
now: You follow end-times videos online with real interest. But the Prophet ﷺ pointed the signs back at deeds. {idea}The question is not when it comes, but what you do now.{/idea}
old: Signs of the end are interesting things to know about.
new: Every sign of the end is a call to hurry toward good deeds today.
try: Do one good deed today that you have been putting off.

title: From every nation, a group gathered and driven.
subtitle: Deniers brought forward on the Day
then: Ibn Kathir describes {trap}the wrongdoers who disbelieved in the signs and Messengers being gathered before Allah{/trap}, a group from every people and generation. He links it to the verse about the wrongdoers being assembled with their companions.
now: Who you spend your evenings with shapes who you become. The friends you laugh with at wrong things. {idea}On that Day, people stand with their kind.{/idea} You can choose your company now.
old: Who I hang out with does not change who I am.
new: I will be gathered with the people I chose to walk with, so I should choose well.
try: Spend time today with one person who reminds you of Allah.

title: You denied what you never understood?
subtitle: The question at the place of reckoning
then: Ibn Kathir explains that standing before Allah, {trap}they will be asked about their beliefs and their deeds.{/trap} The question points out they rejected signs they never tried to understand.
now: You dismissed something about faith because of a meme, a bad experience, a headline. {trap}You rejected it without ever studying it.{/trap} The question will be: did you even look? And what did you do?
old: I can dismiss what I have not studied if it does not feel right.
new: I will be asked whether I really looked before I rejected, and what I did with what I knew.
try: Pick one question about your faith you have avoided. Look up a reliable answer today.

title: No excuse left, and no words to say.
subtitle: Speechless before the One who sees
then: Ibn Kathir says {trap}they will be stunned and speechless, unable to give any answer{/trap}, because they wronged themselves in the world and have now returned to the One from Whom nothing is hidden. He cites the verse that they will not be permitted to give excuses.
now: You have a ready explanation for most things: tired, busy, stressed, everyone does it. {idea}Excuses work on people.{/idea} The time to fix things is while words can still turn into change.
old: I will be able to explain my reasons when the time comes.
new: The time for explaining and changing is now, not on the Day.
try: Drop one excuse you use often. Do the thing instead, once, today.

title: Night for rest, day for sight.
subtitle: A daily sign everyone lives inside
then: Between scenes of the Day, Allah points to everyday life. Ibn Kathir explains the darkness of night lets people {reward}halt their activities and calm down to recover from the day{/reward}, and day is filled with light so they can {reward}work, travel and earn a living.{/reward}
now: You scroll in bed until 2am, then drag yourself through the morning. {idea}Night was made for rest.{/idea} Respecting the rhythm Allah made is a kind of gratitude.
old: Night is just extra time for screens.
new: Night and day are signs made for my rest and my work, and I can honor both.
try: Put your phone away 30 minutes earlier tonight and rest.

title: The Horn is blown, and all come humbled.
subtitle: The Day everyone answers the call
then: Ibn Kathir says the Horn will be blown by the angel Israfil, {trap}signaling the end of this world.{/trap} Everyone will be terrified except whom Allah wills, which he says are {reward}the martyrs, alive with their Lord.{/reward} All come to Him {idea}humbling themselves and obeying.{/idea}
now: You flinch at a loud alarm, a sudden siren on the street. Imagine a sound that stops every phone, every meeting, every argument at once. {idea}Every person walking toward Him, humbled.{/idea} Humility now is practice for then.
old: Some people are too important to be humbled.
new: Everyone will come to Allah humbled, so I can choose humility now.
try: In your next sajdah, stay a few extra seconds and feel how small you are before Him.

title: Mountains that seem fixed will drift like clouds.
subtitle: Nothing solid stays forever
then: Ibn Kathir explains you see the mountains {idea}as if they are fixed and will remain{/idea}, but they will move like clouds. It is the work of Allah who perfected all He created, and {idea}He knows all His servants do, good or evil.{/idea}
now: Your career, your house, the life you have built: it all feels like a mountain. {idea}Even mountains will drift.{/idea} The only thing that lasts is what you did, which He already knows.
old: The solid things in my life will always be there.
new: Even what seems most permanent will pass, so I should invest in what lasts.
try: Look at the sky or a hill today and remind yourself it will pass, but your deeds remain.

title: Bring good, receive better, and be safe.
subtitle: The reward for sincere good
then: Qatadah said the good deed is {idea}sincerely for Allah alone.{/idea} Ibn Kathir notes Allah explained elsewhere that {reward}He will give ten like it{/reward}, and that such people will be safe from the terror of that Day, untouched by the greatest terror.
now: You helped a neighbor carry groceries. You paid for a stranger's coffee. You held your tongue when you wanted to snap. {reward}Done for Allah, each one comes back multiplied.{/reward} And on the hardest Day, it becomes safety.
old: Small good deeds do not add up to much.
new: Every sincere good deed comes back better and brings me safety on the Day.
try: Do one small good deed today purely for Allah, and tell no one.

title: Repaid only for what you used to do.
subtitle: The other side of the scale
then: Ibn Kathir says this is for {trap}whoever comes to Allah with evil deeds and no good deeds, or whose evil outweighs their good.{/trap} They are told: {idea}are you being repaid for anything except what you used to do?{/idea}
now: The habit you keep returning to. The person you keep hurting. {idea}What you used to do is what you will meet.{/idea} The hopeful side: you can start adding good to the scale today.
old: My bad habits are small and will not really count against me.
new: I will meet exactly what I used to do, so I can start changing the balance now.
try: Pair one bad habit with one good deed today, every time it shows up.

title: I am only commanded to worship the Lord of this city.
subtitle: The Prophet ﷺ states his mission
then: Ibn Kathir says linking Lord to this city is {reward}a sign of honor and divine care{/reward} for Makkah. He cites the Prophet ﷺ on the day of the conquest: {idea}this city was made sacred by Allah the day He created the heavens and the earth.{/idea}
now: You face the qiblah five times a day, from your bedroom, your office, an airport corner. {idea}Your direction points to one sacred city, but the Lord of it owns everything.{/idea} Your whole life is His.
old: Worship is for the mosque and special places.
new: The Lord of the sacred city owns everything, so every part of my life is for Him.
try: At your next prayer, pause as you face the qiblah and remember who owns everything.

title: Recite it. Guidance helps the one who takes it.
subtitle: The warner's job, and its limit
then: The Prophet ﷺ is told to recite the Quran to people {idea}so as to convey it{/idea}. Ibn Kathir says he had an example in the Messengers who warned their people, and Allah would do the judging, as another verse says: {idea}your duty is only to convey.{/idea}
now: You share a verse in the family group, give a gentle reminder at dinner. Some respond, some roll their eyes. {idea}Your part is to say it well.{/idea} What they do with it is between them and Allah.
old: If people do not change after I remind them, I have failed.
new: My job is to convey kindly; guidance benefits whoever accepts it.
try: Share one verse you love with someone today, with no expectation.

title: Praise Allah. You will see His signs.
subtitle: How the surah closes
then: The surah ends with praise to Allah, {idea}who does not punish anyone except after establishing proof and warning.{/idea} He will show His signs. Ibn Kathir notes Imam Ahmad used to recite: {idea}if you are alone one day, do not say I am alone; say someone is watching me.{/idea}
now: Late at night, the house quiet, phone in hand, no one around. {idea}You are never really alone.{/idea} That is not a threat. It is the closing comfort of a surah full of His signs.
old: When no one is around, what I do does not really matter.
new: Allah is never unaware of me, and I will keep recognizing His signs if I look.
try: Tonight, when you are alone, say al-hamdu lillah and remember He is with you.
